section.title: Django vs Flask vs FastAPI — Python Frameworks
section.subtitle: Batteries-included vs micro vs async — routing, requests, responses, templates, ORM, auth, validation, async and deployment.

django.definition: Django is batteries-included: ORM, admin, auth, forms, templates, migrations and security all built in. Opinionated structure (projects/apps) for large, structured apps.
django.code:
pip install django
django-admin startproject mysite
python manage.py startapp blog

# You get: ORM, admin site, auth, CSRF,
# migrations, templating — out of the box.

flask.definition: Flask is a micro-framework: routing, request/response and Jinja2 templating only. You assemble everything else (ORM, auth, forms) from extensions — maximum flexibility.
flask.code:
pip install flask

from flask import Flask
app = Flask(__name__)

# You choose: SQLAlchemy, Flask-Login,
# Flask-WTF, Celery… — glue it yourself.

fastapi.definition: FastAPI is modern and async-first: automatic interactive docs, Pydantic validation, type hints as the API contract, and native async/await performance.
fastapi.code:
pip install fastapi uvicorn

from fastapi import FastAPI
app = FastAPI()   # /docs UI auto-generated

# Type hints drive validation + OpenAPI schema.

django.definition: Fixed convention: a project (settings/urls/wsgi) containing apps, each with models.py, views.py, urls.py, admin.py, migrations/ — enforced layout.
django.code:
mysite/
├── manage.py
├── mysite/          # settings.py, urls.py, wsgi.py
└── blog/            # an app
    ├── models.py
    ├── views.py
    ├── urls.py
    ├── admin.py
    └── migrations/

flask.definition: No enforced structure — a single app.py works, or you grow into blueprints (modular route groups) with templates/ and static/ folders.
flask.code:
myapp/
├── app.py
├── config.py
├── models.py
├── routes/          # or blueprints
│   ├── auth.py
│   └── api.py
├── templates/
└── static/

# Factory pattern recommended for larger apps.

fastapi.definition: Flexible layout — typically main.py plus routers/ modules for grouping endpoints. Depends on how you organise; no required conventions.
fastapi.code:
app/
├── main.py          # FastAPI() + include_router
├── routers/
│   ├── users.py
│   └── items.py
├── models.py       # Pydantic schemas
├── database.py     # engine + session
└── auth.py         # dependencies

# Routers keep files focused.

django.definition: urls.py uses path()/re_path() with converters like <int:id>. URLconf includes app urlconfs hierarchically; views return HttpResponse.
django.code:
# blog/urls.py
from django.urls import path
from . import views

urlpatterns = [
    path('posts/<int:post_id>/', views.post_detail),
    path('posts/', views.post_list),
]

# mysite/urls.py includes: path('blog/', include('blog.urls'))

flask.definition: Decorators (@app.route) bind URL patterns to functions directly — converters like <int:id> in the path string. Blueprints prefix groups of routes.

fastapi.definition: Decorators (@app.get/@app.post…) on async functions; path params typed via function signature. APIRouter groups endpoints with prefixes.

topics.title: Reading Request Data
topics.learn: Path params, query strings, JSON bodies, form data.

django.definition: request.GET for query params, request.POST for form data, request.body for raw body; json.loads(request.body) for JSON. CSRF enforced on POST.
django.code:
def create_post(request):
    if request.method == 'POST':
        # JSON body
        data = json.loads(request.body)
        title = data.get('title')
        # form data
        # title = request.POST.get('title')
    # query: request.GET.get('page')

flask.definition: request.args (query), request.form (form), request.get_json() or request.json (JSON body), request.files for uploads.

fastapi.definition: Parameters declared in the signature: path params, Query(...) defaults, and Pydantic models for the JSON body — parsed & validated automatically.
fastapi.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel

class PostIn(BaseModel):
    title: str
    body: str | None = None

@router.post('/posts')
async def create(
    data: PostIn,                          # JSON body, validated
    draft: bool = Query(False),           # ?draft=true
    q: str = ''                           # ?q=search
):
    return data

django.definition: JsonResponse(data) returns JSON; render(request, template) returns HTML; HttpResponse/redirect/status codes control the rest.

flask.definition: jsonify() serialises dicts/lists; render_template() for HTML; make_response/Response for headers, cookies and status codes.

fastapi.definition: Return Python dicts/lists/models directly — FastAPI serialises to JSON automatically. response_model validates outgoing shape; Response for custom headers/status.

django.definition: Django Templates is built in: {{ vars }}, {% tags %}, {% extends %} inheritance, automatic XSS escaping, template tags & filters.
django.code:
{% extends "base.html" %} {% block content %}

{{ post.title }}

{{ post.body|truncatewords:30 }}

{% for c in post.comments.all %}

{{ c.author }}: {{ c.text }}

{% endfor %} {% endblock %}

flask.definition: Jinja2 ships with Flask: {{ vars }}, {% for/if %}, template inheritance via {% extends %}/{% block %}, autoescaping for .html files.
flask.code:
{% extends "base.html" %} {% block content %}

{{ post.title }}

{% for c in post.comments %}

{{ c.author }}: {{ c.text }}

{% endfor %} {% endblock %} # render_template('post.html', post=post)

fastapi.definition: FastAPI doesn't ship HTML templating — use Jinja2Templates manually, or return JSON and let a frontend (React/Vue) render. API-first by design.

django.definition: Built-in ORM: models are Python classes; queries look like Python (objects.filter(...)); migrations auto-generated via makemigrations/migrate.
django.code:
# models.py
class Post(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    author = models.ForeignKey(User, on_delete=models.CASCADE)

# views.py
posts = Post.objects.filter(author=user).order_by('-pub_date')[:5]
post = Post.objects.get(id=1)

# migrations
# python manage.py makemigrations && migrate

flask.definition: No built-in ORM — use SQLAlchemy (via Flask-SQLAlchemy) for models, sessions and migrations (Flask-Migrate/Alembic), or raw sqlite3/psycopg.
flask.code:
from flask_sqlalchemy import SQLAlchemy
db = SQLAlchemy(app)

class Post(db.Model):
    id = db.Column(db.Integer, primary_key=True)
    title = db.Column(db.String(200))

# query
posts = Post.query.filter_by(author_id=1).all()

# migrations: flask db migrate && flask db upgrade

fastapi.definition: Choose your ORM: SQLAlchemy 2.0 (async supported), Tortoise ORM, or Beanie (MongoDB). SQLModel blends Pydantic + SQLAlchemy — popular for FastAPI.
fastapi.code:
# SQLModel example
class Post(SQLModel, table=True):
    id: int | None = Field(default=None, primary_key=True)
    title: str

async def get_post(session, id):
    return await session.get(Post, id)

# raw SQL also easy via text() / asyncpg

django.definition: Built-in auth system: User model, login/logout views, session auth, password hashing, @login_required decorator, groups & permissions.

flask.definition: Via extensions: Flask-Login manages sessions & @login_required; Flask-JWT-Extended issues JWT tokens for APIs; Werkzeug handles password hashing.
flask.code:
from flask_login import LoginManager, login_user, login_required
from werkzeug.security import generate_password_hash

@login_required
def dashboard(): ...

# JWT alternative:
# @jwt_required()
# current_user = get_jwt_identity()

fastapi.definition: Security via dependencies: OAuth2PasswordBearer for JWT, passlib/bcrypt for hashing, and Depends() to inject the current user into endpoints.
fastapi.code:
from fastapi.security import OAuth2PasswordBearer
from jose import jwt

oauth2 = OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl='token')

async def current_user(token: str = Depends(oauth2)):
    payload = jwt.decode(token, SECRET, algorithms=['HS256'])
    return await db.get_user(payload['sub'])

@router.get('/me')
async def me(user = Depends(current_user)):
    return user

topics.title: Input Validation
topics.learn: Checking that incoming data is correct.

django.definition: Forms (django.forms / ModelForm) validate POST data with field validators, clean() methods and is_valid(); DRF serializers do the same for APIs.

flask.definition: Manual checks or WTForms/Flask-WTF: form classes declare fields & validators; form.validate_on_submit() gates the view logic.

fastapi.definition: Pydantic models validate automatically — wrong types or missing fields return 422 with detailed errors before your code runs. Field() adds constraints.
fastapi.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, EmailStr

class SignupIn(BaseModel):
    email: EmailStr
    password: str = Field(min_length=8)
    age: int = Field(ge=0, le=120)

@router.post('/signup')
async def signup(data: SignupIn):
    # already validated — types guaranteed
    ...

# invalid input → automatic 422 response

django.definition: Django is synchronous WSGI by default — one request blocks a worker thread. ASGI support exists (Django 3.0+) for async views, but the ORM is largely sync.

flask.definition: Flask is synchronous — each request occupies a thread. Async views exist (Flask 2.0+) for async libraries, but extensions often aren't async-ready.
flask.code:
@app.route('/feed')
def feed():   # sync — blocks thread
    data = requests.get('https://api.example.com').json()
    return jsonify(data)

# scale with gunicorn workers:
# gunicorn -w 4 app:app
# Flask 2.x: async def view() for aiohttp etc.

fastapi.definition: FastAPI is async-native on ASGI (uvicorn): async def endpoints handle thousands of concurrent connections without thread-per-request overhead.
fastapi.code:
@router.get('/feed')
async def feed():   # non-blocking
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as c:
        r = await c.get('https://api.example.com')
    return r.json()

# one process handles many concurrent requests
# uvicorn main:app --workers 4

topics.title: Middleware & Dependencies
topics.learn: Cross-cutting logic: logging, auth, CORS, DB sessions.

django.definition: Middleware classes process every request/response in settings.MIDDLEWARE order. Decorators (@login_required) and context processors add per-view logic.
django.code:
# settings.py
MIDDLEWARE = [
    'django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware',
    'django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware',
    'corsheaders.middleware.CorsMiddleware',
    'django.middleware.common.CommonMiddleware',
    # ...
]

# custom: class MyMW: def __call__(self, request): ...

flask.definition: before_request/after_request decorators run around every request; @app.errorhandler catches exceptions; extensions plug in CORS, sessions.

fastapi.definition: Depends() injects shared logic (DB sessions, current user, settings) into any endpoint; middleware via @app.middleware('http') wraps all requests.
fastapi.code:
async def get_db():
    async with Session() as s:
        yield s   # dependency with cleanup

@router.get('/users')
async def list_users(db = Depends(get_db)):
    return await db.exec(select(User))

@app.middleware('http')
async def log(req, call_next):
    resp = await call_next(req)
    print(req.url.path, resp.status_code)
    return resp

topics.title: Testing & Deployment
topics.learn: Test frameworks and how each ships to production.

django.definition: Built-in test runner (unittest-style TestCase) with test client, fixtures and DB isolation. Deploy via gunicorn+nginx or PaaS; DEBUG=False in prod.
django.code:
# tests.py
from django.test import TestCase, Client

class PostTests(TestCase):
    def test_list(self):
        r = Client().get('/posts/')
        self.assertEqual(r.status_code, 200)

# run: python manage.py test
# deploy: gunicorn mysite.wsgi:application

flask.definition: pytest + pytest-flask or unittest; test_client simulates requests. Deploy with gunicorn/waitress behind nginx, Docker, or serverless.
flask.code:
def test_home(client):
    resp = client.get('/')
    assert resp.status_code == 200

def test_create_post(client):
    resp = client.post('/posts', json={'title': 'Hi'})
    assert resp.status_code == 201

# deploy: gunicorn -w 4 'app:app'

fastapi.definition: pytest + httpx AsyncClient/TestClient; dependency_overrides for mocking. Deploy with uvicorn/gunicorn workers, Docker, or serverless ASGI hosts.
fastapi.code:
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
client = TestClient(app)

def test_users():
    r = client.get('/users')
    assert r.status_code == 200

# async variant: httpx.AsyncClient(transport=ASGITransport(app=app))
# deploy: uvicorn main:app --workers 4

topics.title: When to Choose Which
topics.learn: Decision guide for picking a framework.

django.definition: Choose Django for large content sites, admin-heavy apps, teams wanting convention over configuration, or when you need auth/admin/forms/ORM without assembling them.
django.code:
# Pick Django when:
# - CMS, e-commerce, dashboards
# - need admin panel out of the box
# - team prefers explicit structure
# - monolith with many built-in features
# Examples: Instagram, Pinterest, Dropbox

flask.definition: Choose Flask for small APIs, prototypes, microservices, or when you want full control over every component. Great learning tool and for teams who like flexibility.
flask.code:
# Pick Flask when:
# - small/medium APIs & services
# - microservices architecture
# - you want to choose every library
# - simple apps that don't need Django's weight
# Examples: Netflix (historically), LinkedIn, Reddit (parts)

fastapi.definition: Choose FastAPI for modern async APIs, high-performance microservices, auto-generated docs (Swagger/Redoc), type-safe contracts, and ML/data backends.
fastapi.code:
# Pick FastAPI when:
# - async/high-throughput APIs
# - auto docs for frontend teams
# - Pydantic validation matters
# - ML/AI services, data pipelines
# Examples: Uber, Microsoft, Netflix (internal tools)
